# A. Assignment Cost

## How to find it

Maintain feasible Hungarian potentials and augment only through equality edges.

## Correctness

Reduced costs stay nonnegative, giving a dual lower bound. The final perfect matching uses tight edges and reaches the bound.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

Here the rectangular Hungarian implementation runs in `O(n squared m)` for
`n` rows and `m` columns, with `n <= m`, and uses `O(n+m)` auxiliary storage.
The potentials are a verifiable optimality certificate: every reduced cost is
nonnegative and every selected edge is tight.

# B. Forbidden Profit Assignment

## How to find it

Negate profits and encode forbidden pairs by a dominant infinity.

## Correctness

Finite assignments preserve reversed objective order; an infinity edge occurs exactly when no complete allowed assignment exists.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

The sentinel must exceed the largest possible difference between two finite
assignment totals. After Hungarian finishes, inspect the selected original
pairs; a sentinel in the result means that no all-allowed complete assignment
exists. The running time is `O(n squared m)`.

# C. General Pairing

## How to find it

Contract odd alternating cycles between even BFS vertices.

## Correctness

Blossom contraction preserves augmenting-path existence, and expansion of predecessors yields a valid original path whose flip grows the matching.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

With the adjacency-matrix-style blossom implementation, at most `n`
augmentations each take `O(n squared)`, for `O(n cubed)` time and `O(n squared)`
graph storage. A triangle, a blossom with a tail, and nested odd cycles are the
minimum useful structural tests.

# D. Compatibility Pairing

## How to find it

Build exactly the allowed compatibility graph and run general matching.

## Correctness

Valid disjoint pair families are precisely graph matchings, so their optima coincide.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

Building the graph is linear in the declared compatible pairs; the blossom
phase is `O(n cubed)`. Check the parity of `n`, but do not confuse even size
with guaranteed feasibility: the matching must still cover every vertex.

# Upsolving checklist

For assignment, compare with all permutations for tiny rectangular matrices.
For general matching, enumerate every choice of disjoint edges. Include ties,
negative profits, isolated vertices, parallel descriptions of the same pair,
and cases in which the first locally attractive pair prevents a perfect
matching. These oracles test the reduction and objective, not merely whether
the produced pairs are disjoint.
